name: Joseon Korea
title: Social Hierarchy of Joseon Korea: From King to Enslaved

tiers.name: The king
tiers.you: You rule with the advice of the State Council and must hear the censors, who can demand that you withdraw your decrees; if you defy the scholar-officials too far, they may depose you.
tiers.kid: Joseon kings ruled with the help of scholar-officials, and King Sejong gave Korea its own alphabet, hangul.
tiers.rise: The throne passed within the royal Yi family to a son or another kinsman, not always peacefully: Grand Prince Suyang seized it from his nephew Danjong and reigned as Sejo from 1455, and the officials who deposed Yeonsangun in 1506 chose his half-brother.
tiers.why: The king (wang) stood at the head of the state and of its Confucian order.

tiers.name: Yangban
tiers.you: You study the Confucian classics for the examinations that open the road to office, your family’s name stands in the local register of yangban lineages, and slaves work your land.
tiers.kid: Yangban were Korea’s ruling families, whose sons studied for years to pass the government exams.
tiers.rise: In theory any free man could sit the examinations, and a family that produced no official for several generations lost its status, though the rule seems never to have been enforced, and yangban sons, who could study for years, won almost all the degrees. After the Japanese invasions of the 1590s the state sold titles and blank certificates of office for grain, and status was increasingly bought.
tiers.why: The yangban, the “two orders” of civil (munban) and military (muban) officials, were the ruling class.

tiers.name: Middle people
tiers.term: jungin (chungin), hyangni (local clerks), seoeol (sons of concubines)
tiers.you: You serve the government as an interpreter or a physician, as your father did, after passing the miscellaneous examination that the yangban look down on, and it opens only the lower ranks to you.
tiers.kid: The “middle people” were Korea’s interpreters, doctors and clerks, who passed their own special exams.
tiers.rise: Status passed from father to son, and the miscellaneous examinations kept the technical posts within the same families. King Jeongjo opened a door in the late 18th century, appointing sons of concubines as scholars in his royal library, the Gyujanggak.
tiers.why: Between the yangban and the commoners stood the jungin, the “middle people”: the hereditary technical specialists of the government and their families.

tiers.name: Commoners
tiers.you: You farm a few fields, pay the land tax and the local tribute, and owe the state military service or a tax in cotton cloth; the law lets you sit the examinations, but you cannot spare the years of study.
tiers.kid: Most Koreans were farmers, and by law ordinary people had to wear plain white clothes.
tiers.rise: A rich commoner could buy a post, a title or a forged genealogy, and so many did that in the registers of Daegu nearly 70 per cent of the people were listed as yangban by 1858. Debt and famine pushed others into slavery.
tiers.why: Most Koreans were commoners (sangmin), the free “good people” (yangin) of the law: farmers above all, with artisans, merchants and fishermen.

tiers.name: Enslaved people
tiers.you: You belong to a yangban family that can sell you or give you away; you farm a plot of your own apart from your master’s house and hand him the harvest of another, but whatever you own goes back to him when you die.
tiers.kid: Enslaved people, called nobi, were owned by others and had to work for them; their children were born enslaved too.
tiers.rise: Nobi could buy their freedom, earn it by military service or receive it from the state, and many ran away. The system declined from the 18th century: most government nobi were freed in 1801, hereditary slavery was abolished in 1886 and all slavery with the Gabo Reforms of 1894.
tiers.why: The nobi were the core of the lowborn (cheonmin), and in the 15th to 17th centuries, the system’s height, they made up at least 30 per cent of the people.

tiers.name: Outcasts
tiers.you: You slaughter animals and tan their hides in a settlement set apart from your neighbours; outside your house you must wear a bamboo hat, you may not wear silk or live under a tiled roof, and you have no surname.
tiers.kid: Butchers and some other workers were treated as outcasts and had to live apart from other people.
tiers.rise: There was almost no way out: outcast status was inherited, and the baekjeong could not sit the examinations. Their legal disabilities ended only with the Gabo Reforms of 1894, and discrimination lasted far longer.
tiers.why: Beside the nobi among the lowborn stood groups despised for their work rather than owned.
